extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Kant's Critique of Judgment; general readers of Project Gutenberg eBooks
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and summarize Kant's criteria for aesthetic and teleological judgement (what counts as a true aesthetic/teleological judgement, limits of analogical inference, moral/teleological role of Nature) together with the Project Gutenberg distribution requirements appended to the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement (disinterested satisfaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: We view beautiful nature with favour, whilst we have a quite free (disinterested) satisfaction in its form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An aesthetic judgement is characterized by disinterested pleasure in form: it does not take into account the purpose for which natural beauties exist (whether to excite pleasure in us or as purposes without reference to us). The disinterested character of the judgement is the key criterion distinguishing aesthetic from other kinds of judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological judgement (consideration of purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a teleological judgement we pay attention to [nature's] reference [to us or purposes], and here we can regard it as a favour of nature that it has been willing to minister to our culture by the exhibition of so many beautiful figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teleological judgement explicitly considers purposes or ends in nature. Unlike mere aesthetic judgement, it assesses natural forms with respect to purposiveness and possible relations to human ends or cultural uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organisational purposiveness judged by Idea of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Every member should surely be purpose as well as means, and, whilst all work together towards the possibility of the whole, each should be determined as regards place and function by means of the Idea of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judging an organised body (biological organisation, etc.) requires conceiving parts in relation to an Idea of the whole; the purposiveness of members is determined by their role for the whole. For intellect, conception of an organised body presupposes the Idea of design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of analogy in inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy (in a qualitative signification) is the identity of the relation between reasons and consequences... we can conclude according to analogy that beasts too act in accordance with representations ... but cannot therefore conclude that the beaver must have reason like man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical reasoning is legitimate when there is an identity of the relation between causes and effects (par ratio). It permits inferring similar modes of operation where grounds are comparable, but it does not license transferring specific properties across fundamentally different genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paritas rationis requirement for analogical inference to persons/Deity
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot ... conclude according to analogy to those properties in [man] [which are in man], because here the principle of the possibility of such a method of reasoning entirely fails, viz. the paritas rationis for counting the Supreme Being in one and the same genus with man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogical arguments to a Supreme Being fail when there is no parity of reasons (paritas rationis) between the compared subjects. One may compare effects to infer a kind of purposiveness, but cannot legitimately infer shared inner properties (e.g., attributes of a Deity) from analogy where generic equivalence is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical examination of speculative (dogmatic) assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: It only remains for us, if the need should arise, to abandon all these objective assertions and to examine critically our judgement merely in reference to our cognitive faculties, in order to supply to their principle a validity which, if not dogmatic, shall at least be that of a maxim sufficient for the sure employment of Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When faced with dogmatic speculative answers, one should suspend objective assertions and instead examine judgments with respect to the limits and conditions of our cognitive faculties; aim for principles that secure Reason's legitimate use rather than dogmatic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical constraint on generative hypotheses (generatio types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generatio univoca (one organic being from another different one) is not absurd a priori, but experience gives no example; according to experience all generation that we know is generatio homonyma (product similar to producer). Generation heteronyma is nowhere found in our empirical knowledge of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypotheses about radical transformations of species may be logically possible a priori, but empirical standard requires that we rely on observed regularities (generation produces like kinds). Empirical absence of heteronyma constrains acceptance of speculative generative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: things of faith vs articles of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Things of faith are not therefore articles of faith; if we understand by the latter things of faith to the confession of which (internal or external) we can be bound. Natural theology contains nothing like this. For since they, as things of faith (like things of fact) cannot be based on theoretical proofs, [they are accepted by] a belief which is free and which only as such is compatible with the morality of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In natural theology certain propositions must be accepted as 'things of faith' that cannot be proven theoretically; these are not binding articles (confessional obligations) but free beliefs that remain compatible with moral autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral final purpose vs happiness (criterion for final purpose of creation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is only as a moral being that man can be the final purpose of creation; happiness, on the contrary, is not even a purpose of nature in respect of man in preference to other creatures; much less a final purpose of creation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asking for the objective 'final purpose' of creation, the relevant criterion is moral worth (man under moral laws), not subjective happiness. Happiness may be a conditioned purpose for individuals, but the moral law determines the highest purposive status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral necessity of assuming God/immortality (practical requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: This moral argument does not supply any objectively-valid proof of the Being of God; it does not prove to the sceptic that there is a God, but proves that if he wishes to think in a way consonant with morality, he must admit the assumption of this proposition under the maxims of his practical Reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculative Reason cannot provide objective proof of God or immortality; however, for practical moral reason (to avoid contradiction with morality) one must adopt these ideas as regulative assumptions — they are necessary for the practical coherence of moral agency, not proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fides (trust in moral law) as moral-assumptive criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The word fides expresses this; ... a trust in the promise of the moral law; ... a final purpose cannot be commanded by any law of Reason without this latter at the same time promising, however uncertainly, its attainableness; and thus justifying our belief in the special conditions under which alone our Reason can think it as attainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral action requires a practical trust (fides) that the moral law's ends are at least conditionally attainable; this trust functions as a subjective but morally necessary assumption that grounds practical commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of life judged by purposive action not mere enjoyment
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of life for us, if it is estimated by that which we enjoy (happiness), is easy to decide. It sinks below zero.... There remains then nothing but the value which we ourselves give our life, through what we can not only do, but do purposively in such independence of nature...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion for the worth of life: do not base it solely on enjoyment (happiness); rather value lies in purposive actions in accordance with moral ends and independence from mere natural inclinations.
